word:lxx:L700031.explanation: Abdia is a personal name, also rendered Avthia. It identifies people in the Old Testament Greek Scriptures rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in genealogical and historical sections from 1 Chronicles through Nehemiah. Because the available passages do not include their verse text here, the particular identity of each person must be determined from its surrounding passage. Its central meaning is therefore its use as the name Abdia or Avthia.

word:lxx:L700093.explanation: Abram is a proper name—the personal name of the man identified in the Greek Old Testament as Abram. It refers to one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 66 times across 52 verses in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 65 times in Genesis and once in Nehemiah. Its recorded use begins in Genesis 11:26 and ends in Nehemiah 9:7. In some sentences, the name may appear in a possessive expression such as “Abram’s,” but it still identifies Abram.

word:lxx:L700127.explanation: This LXX word is a proper name: “Agarēnos” or “Agarinos.” It identifies a named person or people rather than describing an action, quality, or object, though the lexical information does not identify which. word:lxx:L700152.explanation: Agia, also rendered Ayia, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action word. This name appears 148 times in the Greek LXX corpus, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Its precise referent in any particular verse must be identified from that verse’s surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700523.explanation: This adjective means “irreproachable”: it describes someone who cannot rightly be blamed or charged with wrongdoing. It presents a person as free from valid accusation, not merely as someone who receives popular approval. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:47. That reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain how the word functions in that particular sentence.

word:lxx:L700581.explanation: This verb means to sin through ignorance—that is, to do wrong without full awareness of the offense. It describes the act itself rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 15:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger discussion, but the central idea is wrongdoing committed unintentionally or without knowledge.

word:lxx:L700602.explanation: This verb means “hearken to” or “listen to.” It describes giving attention to what is heard, whether the emphasis is simply on listening or on listening with care. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs five times: once in Isaiah, once in Wisdom, and three times in Sirach. Its basic sense is receptive attention to spoken words or a message; the surrounding verse determines what is being heard and why it matters.

word:lxx:L700677.explanation: Alkatha is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Because the name is preserved as a place name and no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its precise location or significance cannot be explained further from this word alone. Its role is therefore straightforward: Alkatha identifies a named place within the territorial record in Joshua.

word:lxx:L700848.explanation: Ammoni is a proper name identifying an Ammonite person or people. It functions as a personal or group designation rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses, across 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name is rendered “Ammoni,” preserving its identity as a designation connected with Ammon. The exact reference of the name in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L700905.explanation: Anabainō means to step up or ascend.

word:lxx:L701119.explanation: This word describes an action done without mercy or compassion—“mercilessly” or “ruthlessly.” As an adverb, it tells how someone acts or treats another person. Its central idea is harshness that withholds pity, portraying conduct that is severe and unrelenting. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who acts this way and how the action is expressed in each passage.

word:lxx:L701146.explanation: This adjective describes something that is not malleable—something not struck with a hammer or shaped by hammering. word:lxx:L701407.explanation: This adjective means “unharmed” or “unhurt.” It describes someone or something that has not suffered injury, damage, or other harm. word:lxx:L701472.explanation: This verb describes sinking under a weight of misery or succumbing to misfortune. word:lxx:L701551.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “choke” or “drown”—to cause someone or something to lose breath or be overcome by water. word:lxx:L701649.explanation: This adverb means “unexpectedly” or “suddenly,” describing something that happens without being anticipated or with little warning. word:lxx:L701775.explanation: Harmozō means to join or fit together. It can describe instruments being well-tuned or a wife being suited to a man.

word:lxx:L701960.explanation: “Without food” is the meaning of this adverb. It modifies a statement to indicate that food is absent or not being taken, rather than naming a person, object, or place. word:lxx:L703504.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to an account or discourse—a spoken or stated presentation of something. word:lxx:L703773.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “dogma” or “decree”: an established ruling, order, or authoritative instruction. word:lxx:L704260.explanation: The verb means “measure out” or “measure.” It describes determining or assigning a quantity, extent, or amount, and refers to the act of measuring rather than to the measure itself. word:lxx:L704769.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective describes something as “still in the night,” emphasizing the nighttime setting or condition. word:lxx:L704808.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something trembling—shaking with fear, alarm, or intense distress. word:lxx:L704897.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “convict”: to establish or declare that someone is guilty. word:lxx:L705762.explanation: Ephra, also rendered Efra, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:6. word:lxx:L706110.explanation: Tharach, also written Tharakh, is a personal name. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship.
